Nigeria plans to spend $2 billion on a new electricity transmission network designed to increase the country’s capacity to move power across the national grid to at least 19,000 megawatts, as the government seeks to address persistent infrastructure constraints.
The Minister of Power, Joseph Olasunkanmi Tegbe, disclosed the plan during an interview on TVC Breakfast on Monday, saying President Bola Tinubu had approved the project and procurement had commenced.
The proposed East-West Super Grid is expected to be delivered within 18 to 24 months.
“The East-West Grid is going to cost about $2 billion. But again, it will have capacity for us to effectively have at least 19,000 megawatts capacity,” Tegbe said.
The new transmission network will connect Funtua, Gwagwalada, Ikot-Ekpene, Benin, Epe and Ilorin. Tegbe said it would complement the existing national grid rather than replace it, providing additional infrastructure to improve the movement of electricity between generating plants and major consumption centres.
The latest announcement follows reports in October 2025 that Nigeria was negotiating with the Export-Import Bank of China for a $2 billion loan to finance a new super grid .
Former Power Minister Adebayo Adelabu disclosed the discussions at an economic summit in Abuja, saying the proposed financing was intended to support transmission infrastructure linking the country’s eastern and western regions, where many large industrial consumers are located.
According to reports at the time, negotiations with the Chinese lender were advancing after the Federal Executive Council approved the financing proposal.
Adelabu said the project was also intended to encourage industrial users that had disconnected from the unreliable national grid to return to it.
The latest announcement by Tegbe does not establish whether the proposed Chinese loan has been secured or whether the government has arranged an alternative financing structure for the project.
The investment comes as Nigeria continues to struggle with the gap between electricity generation and the amount of power its transmission network can deliver.
Ageing infrastructure, equipment failures and repeated grid disturbances have constrained the reliability of electricity supply .
Tegbe said a technical audit launched shortly after he assumed office identified deficiencies in transmission towers, insulators, conductors and relays across several corridors.
Alongside the proposed super grid, the government is prioritising the rehabilitation of existing transmission infrastructure, including the Oshogbo-Ikeja West line.
Tegbe said restoring the line would increase electricity supply to the Lagos electricity network by 400 megawatts.
“When restored, the line is expected to provide an additional 400 megawatts into the Lagos electricity complex,” he said.
The minister also said the government was working to improve electricity generation, pointing to underutilised power plants operated by the Niger Delta Power Holding Company.
The facilities have more than 3,000 megawatts of installed capacity but currently contribute about 400 megawatts to national supply.

Ghana plans to add a 1,200-megawatt gas-fired power plant to its electricity system, in what would become the country’s largest single generating facility.
